svg.text: One-Way Tables 📊 — the starting point of statistics
Individuals (the items) each have variables (their properties). Together they are data. Knowing each variable's TYPE
controls what math, what charts, and what ML encoding you are allowed to use.
🧱 Individuals, variables, data
Individual = one item in the data set (a person, a thing, a case). Variable = a property of that individual.
Data = individuals + variables. Put it in a table → a data table (usually individuals down the left, variables across the top).
Flavor
Scoops sold
Contains chocolate?
Smooth/chunky?
Vanilla
No

Chocolate
Yes
Smooth
Cookies & Cream
Yes
Chunky
↤ individuals = the flavors (rows)
↥ variables = the columns
🌳 Every variable is one of these types
Variable
Categorical (qualitative)
values are WORDS — yes/no, color, smooth/chunky
Quantitative
values are NUMBERS — height, scoops sold
Discrete — counted, whole steps
scoops sold (no 8.3 scoops)
Continuous — any value
height (5.83 ft, decimals OK)
📏 The 4 levels of measurement — each one adds a new power (Stevens, 1940s)
Going up the ladder, each level keeps everything below it and adds one more thing you can do:
1 · Nominal — just labels, NO order. (colors, names, yes/no, favorite food) [categorical]
2 · Ordinal — labels + ORDER (but gaps are not equal). (terrible < satisfactory < good < awesome) [categorical]
3 · Interval — order + EQUAL gaps, but no true zero (can be negative). (temperature: 50→60 is a real 10° gap) [quantitative]
4 · Ratio — interval + a TRUE zero (can't be negative, ratios make sense). (height, weight, time: 20 kg = twice 10 kg) [quantitative]
🌡️ Interval vs Ratio — the difference, finally clear
The whole difference is ONE thing: does the scale have a TRUE ZERO — a value 0 that means "none of it at all"?
❄️ Interval = NO true zero
0 is just an arbitrary point — it does NOT mean "none".
→ "twice as much" is meaningless; values CAN be negative.
e.g. temperature °C / °F (0°C is just where water freezes)
📏 Ratio = has a TRUE zero (0 = none)
0 really means "nothing at all".
→ "twice as much" works; values are NEVER negative.
e.g. weight, height, time, money (20 kg = twice 10 kg)
🧪 Proof that 40°C is NOT twice 20°C: convert to °F → 20°C = 68°F, 40°C = 104°F.
Now 104 / 68 ≈ 1.53, not 2 — the "twice" broke just by changing units → it was never a real ratio (the fake zero is the culprit).
✅ 3-second test for any column: (1) does 0 mean "none"? (2) does "twice as much" make sense? (3) can it be negative?
YES / YES / NO → ratio · NO / NO / YES → interval.
🌡️ Mind-bender: Kelvin IS ratio (0 K = absolute zero = no heat → 200 K really is twice 100 K), but °C / °F are interval.
Same quantity, different zero → different scale type. (Both still share real differences: a 10° gap is always a 10° gap.)
🧾 What is a "one-way" table — and how to lay it out
A one-way table shows the variables for (usually) one individual. That is why it is called "one-way". When you build one, ask:
do I have more individuals, or more variables? Then orient the table so it fits:
More individuals than variables
Individuals down the left, variables across the top.
(the ice cream table above — 6 flavors, 3 variables)
Each new individual = a new row.
Few individuals, many variables → FLIP it
Individuals across the top, variables down the left.
(compare 2 houses on ~13 features — 2 columns,
many rows; it just fits the page better.)
📡 Why the type matters in real data work (and machine learning)
🔌 The variable type decides how you ENCODE a column for a model (models need numbers)
· Nominal → one-hot encoding (one yes/no column per category — keeps them independent, adds no fake order).
· Ordinal → ordinal / integer encoding (map to 1, 2, 3… and keep the order).
· ⚠️ Trap: giving nominal data numbers like 1, 2, 3 invents a fake order → that is noise that confuses the model.
· It also decides valid stats & charts: categorical → counts, mode, bar charts · quantitative → mean, median, histograms. No "mean of colors".
🔑 The one habit to build:
Before any chart, test, or model, ask of every column: "categorical or quantitative? and which of the 4 levels?"
That single question controls which encoding, which average, which chart, and which statistical test you are allowed to use.
